content.content:
1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.
8	
9	There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.
10

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after the concentrate port 22 has been closed does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

input.summary:
Ledger scope: the disclosure text and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md are identical and are the only authority; brief.md supplied only the title, applicant/inventor (Nimo Rotem), the "Not applicable." cross-reference and government-support entries, the apparatus+method claim classes, and the preserved terms (metering sleeve, dose chamber, flush bypass, index collar, flush poppet, annular rinse channel). prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background cites none, so no citation tracing was required.

Claims: all 20 claims trace. Claim 1's elements (housing with inlet/outlet; metering sleeve defining dose chamber, concentrate port, carrier-liquid admission port, flush bypass opening downstream; annular rinse channel between sleeve outer surface and housing inner surface with a rinse opening through the sleeve; piston with two axially spaced sealing lands and a reduced-diameter waist; piston rod carrying a follower pin; one-way outlet valve; normally closed flush poppet; the fill-position isolation, the close-before-uncover ordering, and the follower-pin rinse that closes before the waist reconnects) each map to explicit disclosure sentences. Dependent claims 2-12 and 15-20 likewise map: two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve; flexible lip on the upstream sealing land; port-edge/land ordering; index collar with helical cam groove turned one increment per full stroke; three axial stop faces; spring-biased detent and three recesses; transparent window and three dose setting numerals; cartridge contents and threaded end cap removable without disturbing the inlet/outlet connections; cylindrical housing with end inlet and opposite-end outlet. Claim 4/16 ("concentrate port closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel communicates with the flush bypass") is an entailment of "The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port," so it is supported. The generalizations in claim 1 ("at least one rinse opening", non-cylindrical housing) are ordinary fallback-ladder breadth authorized by the brief and each disclosed species is claimed in a dependent claim; they are not reported.

Description and summary: every specific relationship traces. The admission port being "at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port" follows necessarily from the disclosed waist-at-concentrate-port fill position plus "the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port". "Supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet" follows from an inline valve whose only carrier source is the inlet. "Withdraws the cartridge along the axis of the dose chamber" follows from a cylindrical housing closed by a threaded end cap. No drafting note, placeholder, open question, unresolved alternative, or internal comment remains anywhere in draft/ (grep for TODO/TBD/placeholder/"by way of example"/"any closed outline"/HTML comments returned nothing). No "by way of example" or open-shape broadening leaked from a figure brief into the application text; the depiction conventions stay confined to figures/.

Numerals: all 29 entries in numerals.md are used consistently, each means one thing, and each appears on at least one sheet. The eight numerals listed in each figure brief match exactly the numerals the detailed description attributes to that figure (FIG. 1: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66; FIG. 2: 18, 20, 22, 24, 30, 32, 34, 38; FIG. 3: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62; FIG. 4: 36, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54). The four view captions in draft/07-drawings.md match the four figure briefs. No named section line is used in any view, so no section-designation mismatch exists.

Figure briefs: the schematic conventions are properly quarantined and disclaimed. FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 disclaim circumferential relationship between ports drawn in different section bands; FIG. 3 disclaims the flare direction of the flexible lip and any discharge direction of the rinse openings; FIG. 4 disclaims which collar end carries the stop faces, their circumferential order, the abutting part, and the hand, pitch and forming surface of the cam groove. Those disclaimers keep the functional faces minimally specific, so they are not reported.

Two defects were found, both in figures/FIG-1.md. First, the brief affirmatively states a flow boundary the inventor never disclosed — that the annular gap between the sleeve and the housing is "interrupted" by the index-collar ring and that "no flow path past that ring is intended" — which also contradicts the description, FIG. 3 and claim 1, all of which require carrier liquid to reach the annular rinse channel from the inlet past that same ring. Second, FIG. 1 simultaneously places the sleeve's left end face against the end cap ring's inner face and the collar ring's left part beyond that same end face, which puts the collar in the space the end cap occupies and cannot be rendered as specified. Both fixes are confined to the figure brief and require no new invention text.

findings.title: FIG. 1 asserts an undisclosed flow boundary at the index collar that contradicts the disclosed rinse path
findings.where: figures/FIG-1.md, Geometry bullets 4 ("The metering sleeve lies inside the housing...") and 9 (final bullet); conflicts with draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶ beginning "The annular rinse channel 60 lies between...", figures/FIG-3.md Geometry bullet 2, and draft/09-claims.md claim 1
findings.detail: The FIG. 1 brief verbalizes two untraced flow-boundary facts about the index collar: that the annular gap between the metering sleeve and the housing is "interrupted" where the collar ring surrounds the sleeve, and that "no flow path past that ring is intended." The inventor never described any sealing, blocking or clearance relationship between the index collar and the housing or the rinse channel; the only statement about the collar is that it "surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin." A statement about a flow boundary is substantive even under a schematic convention, so it must be removed. It is also internally inconsistent: FIG. 1 places the ring in the sleeve/housing annulus at the same (left) end as the inlet, while the description says "The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14", FIG. 3 says the channel is "supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end", and claim 1 requires that "carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel." If no flow can pass the ring, the claimed and described rinse supply is cut off.

Nearest inventor passage, disclosure.md: "An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod." and "Carrier liquid flows through an annular rinse channel between the sleeve and housing". No affirmative passage anywhere in the disclosure or conversation states that the index collar blocks, seals or is sealed from the annular rinse channel, or that flow does or does not pass it.

data.summary:
Ledger scope: the disclosure text and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md are identical and are the only authority; brief.md supplied only the title, applicant/inventor (Nimo Rotem), the "Not applicable." cross-reference and government-support entries, the apparatus+method claim classes, and the preserved terms (metering sleeve, dose chamber, flush bypass, index collar, flush poppet, annular rinse channel). prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background cites none, so no citation tracing was required.

Claims: all 20 claims trace. Claim 1's elements (housing with inlet/outlet; metering sleeve defining dose chamber, concentrate port, carrier-liquid admission port, flush bypass opening downstream; annular rinse channel between sleeve outer surface and housing inner surface with a rinse opening through the sleeve; piston with two axially spaced sealing lands and a reduced-diameter waist; piston rod carrying a follower pin; one-way outlet valve; normally closed flush poppet; the fill-position isolation, the close-before-uncover ordering, and the follower-pin rinse that closes before the waist reconnects) each map to explicit disclosure sentences. Dependent claims 2-12 and 15-20 likewise map: two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve; flexible lip on the upstream sealing land; port-edge/land ordering; index collar with helical cam groove turned one increment per full stroke; three axial stop faces; spring-biased detent and three recesses; transparent window and three dose setting numerals; cartridge contents and threaded end cap removable without disturbing the inlet/outlet connections; cylindrical housing with end inlet and opposite-end outlet. Claim 4/16 ("concentrate port closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel communicates with the flush bypass") is an entailment of "The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port," so it is supported. The generalizations in claim 1 ("at least one rinse opening", non-cylindrical housing) are ordinary fallback-ladder breadth authorized by the brief and each disclosed species is claimed in a dependent claim; they are not reported.

Description and summary: every specific relationship traces. The admission port being "at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port" follows necessarily from the disclosed waist-at-concentrate-port fill position plus "the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port". "Supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet" follows from an inline valve whose only carrier source is the inlet. "Withdraws the cartridge along the axis of the dose chamber" follows from a cylindrical housing closed by a threaded end cap. No drafting note, placeholder, open question, unresolved alternative, or internal comment remains anywhere in draft/ (grep for TODO/TBD/placeholder/"by way of example"/"any closed outline"/HTML comments returned nothing). No "by way of example" or open-shape broadening leaked from a figure brief into the application text; the depiction conventions stay confined to figures/.

Numerals: all 29 entries in numerals.md are used consistently, each means one thing, and each appears on at least one sheet. The eight numerals listed in each figure brief match exactly the numerals the detailed description attributes to that figure (FIG. 1: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66; FIG. 2: 18, 20, 22, 24, 30, 32, 34, 38; FIG. 3: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62; FIG. 4: 36, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54). The four view captions in draft/07-drawings.md match the four figure briefs. No named section line is used in any view, so no section-designation mismatch exists.

Figure briefs: the schematic conventions are properly quarantined and disclaimed. FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 disclaim circumferential relationship between ports drawn in different section bands; FIG. 3 disclaims the flare direction of the flexible lip and any discharge direction of the rinse openings; FIG. 4 disclaims which collar end carries the stop faces, their circumferential order, the abutting part, and the hand, pitch and forming surface of the cam groove. Those disclaimers keep the functional faces minimally specific, so they are not reported.

Two defects were found, both in figures/FIG-1.md. First, the brief affirmatively states a flow boundary the inventor never disclosed — that the annular gap between the sleeve and the housing is "interrupted" by the index-collar ring and that "no flow path past that ring is intended" — which also contradicts the description, FIG. 3 and claim 1, all of which require carrier liquid to reach the annular rinse channel from the inlet past that same ring. Second, FIG. 1 simultaneously places the sleeve's left end face against the end cap ring's inner face and the collar ring's left part beyond that same end face, which puts the collar in the space the end cap occupies and cannot be rendered as specified. Both fixes are confined to the figure brief and require no new invention text.

findings.detail: The FIG. 1 brief verbalizes two untraced flow-boundary facts about the index collar: that the annular gap between the metering sleeve and the housing is "interrupted" where the collar ring surrounds the sleeve, and that "no flow path past that ring is intended." The inventor never described any sealing, blocking or clearance relationship between the index collar and the housing or the rinse channel; the only statement about the collar is that it "surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin." A statement about a flow boundary is substantive even under a schematic convention, so it must be removed. It is also internally inconsistent: FIG. 1 places the ring in the sleeve/housing annulus at the same (left) end as the inlet, while the description says "The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14", FIG. 3 says the channel is "supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end", and claim 1 requires that "carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel." If no flow can pass the ring, the claimed and described rinse supply is cut off.

No affirmative passage anywhere in the disclosure or conversation states that the index collar blocks, seals or is sealed from the annular rinse channel, or that flow does or does not pass it.

findings.detail: The brief states that the cartridge's sleeve end face meets the inner face of the end cap ring seated in the left mouth, and separately that the ring surrounding the sleeve has its left part standing beyond that same sleeve end face. Because the ring surrounds the sleeve, its outer diameter exceeds the sleeve's, so a cap ring whose bore is wide enough to receive the ring's left part cannot also bear on the sleeve's end face, and a cap ring that bears on that end face collides with the ring. As specified the view cannot be rendered consistently, and the contact between the sleeve end face and the cap's inner face is itself narrower than the source, which says only that the cartridge "is retained by a threaded end cap."
